abstract: Neurons can form new representations within a single experience through behavioral-timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP), yet how such rapid learning affects previously established representations remains unclear. We present an analytically tractable theory of BTSP, constrained by experimental measurements in hippocampal CA1, to examine how successive learning events interact within individual neurons. Competition between temporally narrow potentiation and broader, weight-dependent depression generates nonmonotonic interference as a function of the separation between instructive events. Nearby events merge representations, intermediate separations produce the strongest suppression and overwriting, and distant events allow coexistence. This interference arises from the distinct timescales of potentiation and depression rather than the precise functional form of the plasticity kernel. Analytically derived synaptic-weight covariances identify the origin of this constructive-destructive interaction, and a quantitative phase diagram predicts how the transitions between regimes depend on running speed and the spatial tuning of presynaptic inputs. The theory further identifies a velocity-dependent exclusion zone in which the coexistence of distinct representations is strongly suppressed. The effects of new learning therefore depend not only on the animal's current running speed but also on the pre-existing tuning width of presynaptic inputs. Our theory thus predicts the conditions under which new hippocampal place fields merge with, overwrite, or preserve existing representations.
